blocks.text: Every conversation you have with a model lives inside a context window, and that window empties out the moment the session ends. Anything the model needs to carry forward has to be saved somewhere else, on purpose.
Memory management is the discipline of deciding what gets saved, where it gets saved, and how it gets pulled back in later without flooding the context window all over again.
MCP servers are a natural place to put this logic, since they can expose a memory store to any client through simple tools or resources.
1. Short Term Context vs Long Term Memory

blocks.alt: Short term context from the current conversation is compared against long term memory

blocks.text: Short term context is everything currently sitting inside the active conversation, the system prompt, the messages so far, and any tool results from this session.
It is fast, complete, and free to read, but it vanishes the instant the session closes or the context window fills up and older turns get pushed out.
Long term memory is different. It is information deliberately written to storage that outlives the conversation, so a future session can retrieve it.
The two are not competing options, they are complementary layers, short term context handles the moment, long term memory handles continuity across moments.
2. Why Short Term Context Is Not Enough
A user might tell an assistant their preferred coding language on Monday and expect it to still be respected on Friday, in a completely new session.
Without long term memory, every session starts from zero, and the model has no way to know anything happened before this exact moment.
That is fine for a one off question, but it breaks down fast for any assistant meant to feel consistent over days, weeks, or months of use.

blocks.title: Amnesia by default
blocks.content: Unless a system explicitly writes something to persistent storage, a model has no memory of a previous session at all, no matter how important that earlier conversation felt.

blocks.text: 3. What a Memory Store Actually Is
A memory store is just a place outside the model where facts get written and later read back, a database, a file, or a key value store.
It has nothing magical about it, it is closer to a notebook than to the model brain, the model only knows what is in it because something chose to read it in.
4. Exposing Memory Through MCP Resources
One way an MCP server can offer memory is as a resource, a readable item a client can fetch by URI, similar to reading a file.
This works well when memory is meant to be loaded automatically at the start of a session, before the user has asked anything.
5. Exposing Memory Through MCP Tools

blocks.alt: A memory store is exposed to the model through remember and recall tools

blocks.text: The other common approach is to expose memory as tools, typically a remember tool for writing and a recall tool for reading.
Tools fit better when the model needs to decide, mid conversation, that something is worth saving or worth looking up, rather than loading everything up front.

items: A resource is pulled in automatically, usually at session start, without the model asking for it
A tool is called deliberately, whenever the model or the host decides memory needs to be written or read
Many real systems use both, a resource for a starting snapshot and tools for updates during the session

blocks.text: 6. Building a Simple remember Tool

blocks.alt: A remember tool takes a fact and saves it into the memory store

blocks.text: A remember tool takes a piece of information and a user identifier, then writes that fact into the memory store.
Keep the tool narrow, it should save one clear fact at a time, not an entire transcript dumped in as a single blob.
7. Building a Simple recall Tool

blocks.alt: A recall tool queries the memory store and returns matching facts

blocks.text: A recall tool does the opposite, it takes a user identifier and returns whatever facts have been saved for that person.
A basic version just returns everything, but a better version supports a query so only relevant facts come back.
8. A Minimal Memory Server End to End
Put together, a tiny memory server needs only three pieces, storage, a remember tool, and a recall tool.
Everything else in a production system, expiry, summarization, search ranking, builds on top of this same small core.
9. Deciding What Is Worth Remembering
Not everything said in a conversation deserves a permanent home, most of it is only relevant to the moment it happened in.
A good rule of thumb is to ask whether a fact would still change the right answer weeks from now, in a completely different session.

blocks.text: 10. Signals That Something Should Be Saved
A few practical signals help decide, in the moment, whether a piece of information deserves to be written to long term memory.

items: The user explicitly says to remember something for later
The same fact or preference comes up again across multiple turns
The information would be expensive or slow to re derive if lost
The fact describes the user or their setup, rather than the current task

blocks.text: 11. Why Unbounded Memory Becomes a Problem

blocks.alt: Unbounded memory keeps growing until it becomes a problem

blocks.text: If a remember tool is called freely and nothing ever gets removed, the memory store grows without limit, turn after turn, session after session.
Reading all of it back in eventually costs as many tokens as the conversation history it was meant to replace, defeating the whole point.
12. Strategy One: Summarize Before Saving

blocks.alt: A raw entry is summarized before being saved into memory

blocks.text: Instead of saving a full conversation excerpt, condense it into a short factual statement before it ever reaches the memory store.
A summarization step turns a paragraph of chat into one clean line, which is both cheaper to store and cheaper to read back later.

code.content:
def summarize_for_memory(conversation_snippet: str) -> str:
    # in practice this calls a model with a tight instruction,
    # here shown as the shape of the result it should produce
    return "User prefers concise answers with code examples first."

blocks.text: 13. Strategy Two: Cap and Rotate Old Entries
Set a maximum number of facts per user, and when a new one comes in past that cap, drop the oldest or least used entry.
This keeps the memory store bounded no matter how long a user has been active, without needing a human to prune it manually.
14. Strategy Three: Merge Similar Facts
When a new fact overlaps heavily with an existing one, replace the old entry instead of stacking a near duplicate on top.
A memory store that quietly accumulates ten slightly different phrasings of the same preference is just as bloated as one with no limit at all.

items: Before saving, check if a very similar fact already exists for that user
If it does, update or replace it rather than appending a new entry
Only append a brand new entry when the fact is genuinely new information

blocks.text: 15. Strategy Four: Periodic Consolidation
Even with capping and merging, a memory store can slowly fill with many small, related facts that would read better as one summary.
Running an occasional consolidation pass, say once the count crosses a threshold, rewrites many small entries into a few dense ones.

code.content:
def consolidate_if_needed(user_id: str, threshold: int = 30):
    entries = memory_store.get(user_id, [])
    if len(entries) < threshold:
        return
    combined_text = " ".join(e["fact"] for e in entries)
    summary = summarize_for_memory(combined_text)
    memory_store[user_id] = [{"fact": summary, "saved_at": current_timestamp()}]

blocks.text: 16. Retrieving Only What Is Relevant

blocks.alt: Only relevant memory entries are retrieved rather than the whole store

blocks.text: Even a well managed memory store should not be dumped in whole on every session, only the facts relevant to the current task belong in context.
A recall tool that accepts a query, or that ranks facts by relevance, keeps the context window focused instead of pre loading everything just in case.

blocks.title: Recall is a filter, not a dump
blocks.content: Treat the recall tool the same way you would treat any search, return the few facts that matter for this moment, not the entire stored history.

blocks.text: 17. Putting the Pieces Together in a Real Flow
A well behaved session opens by recalling a few relevant facts, works through the conversation using short term context, and closes by remembering anything new and durable.

items: Session starts, host calls recall to load a small set of relevant facts
Conversation proceeds normally using short term context for everything else
Model or host identifies a durable fact worth keeping and calls remember
Memory store applies capping, merging, or consolidation as needed
Next session starts fresh, but recall brings the important facts back

blocks.text: Worked Example
A user tells a coding assistant they always want tests included with any function it writes, across several sessions this week.
The first time this comes up, the assistant calls remember with a short summarized fact rather than the full sentence the user typed.

code.content: remember(user_id="u_42", fact="Always include unit tests with generated functions")

blocks.text: On day two, a new session starts, the host calls recall for user u_42, and this one fact comes back before the user has said anything.
By day five, the user has added three related preferences, so a consolidation pass merges them into one clean entry the next time the cap is checked.
Common Mistakes

items: Saving entire raw conversation transcripts to memory instead of short summarized facts.
Never capping or consolidating memory, so the store grows without bound over months of use.
Loading every stored fact back into context on every session instead of recalling only what is relevant.
Treating short term context and long term memory as the same thing, and assuming the model remembers automatically.
Saving one off details, like a single question, as if they were durable preferences.
Storing near duplicate facts repeatedly instead of merging or updating an existing entry.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
Short term context handles the current conversation, long term memory is a separate store that an MCP server can expose through resources or tools so facts survive past the session.
Good memory management means being selective about what gets saved, and summarizing, capping, or consolidating what is kept so the store never grows into a burden of its own.
